concepts.title: Science Begins with Wonder and Questions

questions.q: Why does science begin with wonder?
questions.a: Noticing puzzles - why do stars twinkle, why does bread rise - starts the questions that science answers.

questions.q: Give one everyday question that science can answer.
questions.a: Why does ice float on water? (Ice is less dense than liquid water.)

questions.q: What does studying science teach us besides facts?
questions.a: It teaches us to observe carefully, test ideas and reason from evidence.

questions.q: What steps does a scientific investigation follow?
questions.a: Observe, question, guess (hypothesise), test with an experiment, record, and conclude.

questions.q: Why must results be recorded honestly?
questions.a: Science depends on truth - false records mislead everyone and collapse when retested.
An experiment where only one factor changes at a time, so its true effect shows.

questions.q: Give one puzzle of daily life that science solved.
questions.a: Why milk sours - microbes ferment it; refrigeration slows them down.

questions.q: Name a question about the sky that science answers.
questions.a: Why day and night alternate - the earth rotates once every 24 hours.

questions.q: How can small puzzles at home lead to big science?
questions.a: Curious questions about mould, rust or shadows lead to experiments, and many discoveries began this way.

concepts.title: Roots and Kites: The Attitude of a Young Scientist

questions.q: What qualities does a young scientist need?
questions.a: Curiosity, patience, honesty, careful observation and the courage to be wrong.

questions.q: Why is it fine for an experiment to fail?
questions.a: Failures remove wrong guesses and teach what to test next - every scientist fails first.

questions.q: What does 'roots and kites' suggest about a scientist's attitude?
questions.a: Stay rooted in evidence and humble, but let imagination fly like a kite while asking questions.
